title: Sonata in A minor for Arpeggione and Piano, “Arpeggione”
hook: Written for a bowed guitar that was soon forgotten, and kept alive by cellists and violists ever since.

painting.title: Viennese Domestic Garden
painting.pairingNote: A quiet Viennese courtyard garden of Schubert’s last years, a woman reading in the shade; the intimate, private Vienna where music like this sonata was played among friends.

facts: Schubert wrote it in Vienna in November 1824, a month after returning from a summer as music teacher to the Esterházy family at Zseliz, then in Hungary (today Želiezovce, Slovakia). It is for the arpeggione, a new instrument built a year or so earlier by the Viennese maker Johann Georg Staufer. It was a kind of bowed guitar: six strings, tuned like a guitar and with frets, held between the knees like a cello and played with a bow.
He wrote it for Vincenz Schuster, a virtuoso on the instrument. The arpeggione never caught on, and Schubert’s sonata is almost the only reason anyone remembers it.

1824 was a hard year for Schubert. He had been seriously ill, and that spring he wrote to his friend Leopold Kupelwieser that he felt himself “the most unhappy and wretched creature in the world”. The sonata’s mood moves between that melancholy and a lighter, almost carefree charm.

It was not published until 1871, long after his death, and by then the arpeggione had fallen out of use. Today it is played on the cello, on the viola, and sometimes on other instruments. Both have four strings instead of six, tuned further apart, so players move some passages up or down an octave and work harder in the fast runs.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a sad, singing Allegro with flashes of virtuosity (I), a short, hymn-like song (II) that leads without a break into a gentle, dancing rondo (III).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The piano begins alone with a sad, gently rocking tune; the cello takes it up and sings it in its warm middle register. A brighter second theme brings quick, playful figures that show off the instrument. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], and in this recording the opening section is played twice.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a melancholy melody in A minor, first in the piano, then in the cello.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a perky, bouncing tune in C major, with quick repeated notes and runs.

mainIdeas.name: The virtuoso figures
mainIdeas.description: fast [[arpeggio|arpeggios]] and scales, the kind of writing that gave the arpeggione its name.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Rostropovich and Britten recorded it at Snape, the concert hall Britten had opened the year before for his Aldeburgh Festival. The two were close friends; Britten wrote his own Cello Sonata and three suites for Rostropovich. Their tempos are slow, and the first movement here is much longer than in most recordings.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A short, simple song in E major. The piano lays down quiet, hymn-like chords, and the cello sings a long melody over them, rising high. The movement does not really end: it pauses on a held note and leads straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a calm, broad melody in the cello, over plain chords in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The link
mainIdeas.description: a few quiet bars that turn towards the finale’s key.

stops.hear: The piano alone: soft, hymn-like chords
The cello sings a long, calm melody above them
The melody climbs higher and grows more intense, with a brief shadow of the minor
The opening melody again, quieter

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music slows and hangs on a held note, then the cello leads on without a pause
stops.happening: The link into the finale, played [[attacca|attacca]]

notice: Listen for the end of the movement. It does not close; it stops on a question, and the finale answers it.

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: A relaxed, good-natured [[rondo|rondo]] in A major. Its main tune is gentle and lilting, and it returns between livelier episodes, one in the minor with energetic leaps and another full of quick runs and broken chords. It ends quietly, without fuss.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, song-like melody in two beats, first in the cello.

mainIdeas.name: The minor-key episode
mainIdeas.description: more energetic, with leaps and strong accents.

mainIdeas.name: The virtuoso episode
mainIdeas.description: rapid runs, arpeggios and plucked notes ([[pizzicato|pizzicato]]).

Darker and more energetic, in the minor, with leaps and accents
The lilting tune again

stops.label: Near the end

notice: Listen to the piano. Even in the cello’s showiest passages, it keeps a light, dancing accompaniment.

threads.title: A forgotten instrument
threads.body: Every bar was written for an instrument almost nobody plays. What we hear is always a translation, and cellists and violists each make it sound like their own instrument’s music.

threads.title: Song
threads.body: Schubert wrote more than six hundred songs, and the sonata often sounds like one: a voice (the cello) over an accompaniment (the piano).

threads.title: Minor and major
threads.body: The sonata starts in A minor and ends in A major, but the major-key finale never forgets the sadness of the opening.
